title: Course Schedule II
statement: There are numCourses courses labelled 0..numCourses-1 and prerequisite pairs [a, b] meaning b must be taken before a. Return any valid order in which all courses can be taken, or an empty array if no such order exists.
realWorld: The compile order a build tool actually emits, not just its yes/no dependency check. Gradle prints the task execution order, npm decides which packages to install first, and a migration runner produces the sequence of scripts to apply.

examples.explanation: 0 has no prerequisites, so it goes first.
[0,2,1,3] is equally valid — 1 and 2 do not depend on each other, so their relative order is free. Any output that respects every edge is accepted.
The two courses require each other, so no ordering exists.

bruteForce.whySlow: It searches the space of permutations. Worse, the backtracking is pointless: if a course is placeable now, placing it can never make another course unplaceable later, so no branch it rules out was ever needed. Twelve courses already exceed 479 million orderings.

patternIdentification: Dependency pairs plus 'return any valid order, or empty if impossible' is the exact signature of a topological sort with cycle detection. This is Course Schedule with the order kept instead of discarded — same loop, different return value.

optimized.idea: Kahn's algorithm. Count how many prerequisites each course still owes, start with all the zeros, and every time a course is emitted decrement its dependents — enqueuing any whose counter reaches zero. The emitted list is the answer; if it is shorter than numCourses the leftovers form a cycle and no order exists.

commonMistakes: Reversing the edge. [a, b] means b -> a; building a -> b produces a plausible but exactly backwards order.
Returning the partial order when a cycle is found. The contract is an empty array — a partial list looks like a valid answer to the caller.
Assuming the expected output is unique and comparing against one specific array. Any order respecting every edge is correct; check the edges, not the sequence.
Seeding the queue with only one root, which silently drops every other component of a disconnected dependency graph.
Sizing the result array with the number of prerequisites instead of numCourses.
